subject: Banking
title: The RJR Nabisco LBO
description: A micro-lesson that makes The RJR Nabisco LBO usable.

hook.text: The 1989 RJR Nabisco buyout at $25 billion was the largest LBO ever at the time.

buildup.text: KKR, a private equity firm, won a bidding war against RJR's own CEO. The deal was financed almost entirely with debt.

discovery.text: The battle revealed that corporate boards could be outbid by financial engineers. Debt could buy what profits could not.

twist.text: KKR struggled to generate returns. The debt burden limited investment. The deal barely broke even after years of effort.

climax.text: RJR Nabisco proved that the biggest deal is not always the best deal.

punchline.text: $25 billion LBO, barely broke even. Winning the bid was losing.

quiz.question: What was the outcome of KKR's record-breaking RJR Nabisco buyout?
options: It barely broke even despite years of effort

details.summary: The 1988 leveraged buyout of RJR Nabisco for 25 billion dollars was the largest LBO in history at the time, immortalized in the book Barbarians at the Gate. It epitomized the 1980s era of aggressive financial engineering and corporate raiding.
details.whyItMatters: RJR Nabisco became the defining deal of the LBO era, exposing how professional buyout firms could acquire massive corporations using borrowed money while enriching themselves at the expense of other stakeholders.
takeaways: KKR won the bidding war with a 25 billion dollar leveraged buyout
The deal used over 20 billion in borrowed money
It became the symbol of 1980s Wall Street excess and greed

faq.question: Why is the RJR Nabisco deal so famous?
faq.answer: The deal combined unprecedented size, competing bidders, management greed, and junk bond financing into a dramatic narrative. The book and HBO movie Barbarians at the Gate made it the most famous deal in Wall Street history.

faq.question: Was the RJR Nabisco LBO a good investment?
faq.answer: Not especially. KKR eventually earned modest returns after years of managing heavy debt loads. The company was broken up over time. The deal proved that the largest LBO is not necessarily the most profitable one.
